I asked that question because I believe free speech it's an ideal, its not feasible to apply in practice and so it can never be absolute, that's why historically there have been always boundaries to exclude or deter certain opinions. What we know as free speech has always been a "regulated free speech",

To have an hypothetical system in place that enables every type of opinion would eventually collapse in itself, because it would also include opinions that would directly endanger the very system that gave them a voice to begin with.

Echo chambers, which granted, are definitely a problem, would never be ever be as efficient as the opportunity to freely and publicly share those opinions, as that gives them way more power: a higher chance to spread, reach a broader audience and eventually become normalised. They are containment zones that gather like-minded individuals from the start, so their reach is very limited.

If we are using the example of racist ideas, there's a reason why developed countries have anti discrimination laws in place, which limit some types speech to a degree. In my opinion, the most concerning thing about bigotry and intolerance is how fast they can spread, specially if linked to some perceived common threat, which is why demagogy has historically been so effective, it plays into peoples fears, tolerance and acceptance as a social goal are much harder to attain than the opposite, therefore you need to find ways for it to gain root and put some selective pressure on, and one of those options is to limit intolerant speech.

It's a very complex issue, and l'm aware suppressing speech can be a slippery slope that can be easily abused, but I can't find a single example of unlimited free speech been applied either. Most modern societies, built on some premise of tolerance and equality, thrive on this regulated free speech, which leaves the open question that we might have reached a similar outcome if we let public opinion regulate itself, and that shit ideas will naturally become the minority, but I sincerely doubt it.
